chapter_plans.title: The First Slip
chapter_plans.one_line_summary: Night-shift nurse Iris Callahan dismisses a stray label printing the name of a child and a time—until the child arrives thirty-five minutes early and dies exactly at 03:47.
chapter_plans.beat_summary: A slow night in the ER breaks when Iris’s label printer activates on its own, producing a slip with 'Lena Zarate – 03:47'. She dismisses it as a malfunction, but when Lena arrives early with respiratory distress, she fights the code alone on the floor — no attending present, Dr. Ovid reachable only by phone if at all. Despite her best efforts, Lena arrests and dies at the exact printed time. Overcome by déjà vu, Iris flashes to the patient death from a year ago that she filed as 'unavoidable' and presses two fingers to her own wrist before she can stop herself.
chapter_plans.opens_with: The label printer shrieked once at 2:10 a.m., then spat out a name no one had entered.
chapter_plans.cliffhanger: Iris reaches behind the counter to unplug the label printer before it can spit out another impossible name—and finds only a smooth plastic back where the power cord should be.

Plant C001 through the printed 'LENA ZARATE – 03:47' incident and C005 through Iris’s involuntary memory of last year’s patient death and pulse-check tic. Include the required no-romance-canon [ROMANCE] micro-beat as isolation/absence (no male lead, no invented doctor). End with the revelation that the printer has no power cord.

chapter_plans.title: A Second Warning
chapter_plans.one_line_summary: When a second label prints and comes true despite Iris's attempts to intervene, she can no longer pretend the machine is ordinary.
chapter_plans.beat_summary: Still shaken after Lena Zarate's death and the powerless printer from the previous shift, Iris returns to the same coastal ER determined to treat the first slip as a stress-induced coincidence. During a tense lull, the machine shrieks to life and spits out a second label: 'ARTHUR BELL — 04:12.' Minutes later, a sixty-year-old man with chest pain is brought in under that name. Iris tries to beat the printed time by putting him in a monitored bed early, calling Dr. Ovid by phone for standing orders, and pushing for aggressive cardiac precautions before the symptoms fully justify them. At 04:12, Arthur arrests anyway, and every intervention fails. After the death, Iris checks the printer and finds the power cord now fully plugged in, contradicting what she saw at the end of the first chapter. She hides the new slip with the old one in her locker, but the first slip has vanished.

chapter_plans.title: The Manufacturer's Mark
chapter_plans.one_line_summary: Iris follows the impossible labels into the hospital archives, where an elderly clerk's evasive memory of a privately owned printer gives her the second clue she needs to realize the machine was never ordinary hospital equipment.
chapter_plans.beat_summary: The blank label with Iris's name still hidden in her pocket, Iris corners Mr. Hanley in the night records room and asks why an ER label printer would have no consistent power source, no asset tag, and a history no one will discuss. Hanley tries to brush her off, but he remembers a similar compact printer from the early 1960s: not hospital-issued, carried in by a nurse whose fascination with patient labels made the old staff uneasy. [CLUE C002] He recalls the machine had a painted-over brass rivet instead of a manufacturer plate, appeared in an old requisition note as 'private equipment,' and was later moved toward the memory care wing after an incident he refuses to describe. When Iris presses him, he abruptly changes the subject and warns her that some records were boxed away for a reason. [ROMANCE] Because there is no true male lead, Iris’s required emotional micro-beat is framed as isolation: she almost wants someone to believe her about the printer, thinks of calling Dr. Ovid (phone only — he will not come), and steadies her own pulse alone. Later, alone with the printer, Iris examines its casing and confirms there is no manufacturer logo, no serial number, no standard hospital asset sticker. Remembering Hanley's comment about the brass rivet, she scrapes at a painted nub near the base. Beneath the paint is a tiny etching: 'Vole, 1963.' She does not know who Vole is and does not connect the name to any living person, but the combination of the first death slip, the second accurate warning, Hanley's memory of private equipment, and the hidden mark forces R001: the printer is not random, not newly placed, and not standard hospital property. Someone connected to the hospital's past brought it here, and now it has found Iris.
chapter_plans.opens_with: “Stop asking about that printer,” Mr. Hanley snapped before Iris had finished saying its name, and the archive key in his hand struck the desk hard enough to make the metal drawers rattle.
chapter_plans.cliffhanger: Iris scrapes the last flake of paint from the brass rivet and reads the etched words 'Vole, 1963.' Before she can copy them down, the dark corridor outside the records room creaks with slow footsteps. She shoves the printer into the bottom drawer and kills the lamp just as the steps stop on the other side of the door.

chapter_plans.title: The Night She Did Nothing
chapter_plans.one_line_summary: Iris tests the new slip by refusing to secretly alter care beyond ordinary triage, and when the patient survives the printed hour, the machine becomes less prophetic and more terrifyingly conditional.
chapter_plans.beat_summary: Iris races back from memory care after the ER call and finds the new label waiting: a patient name, a time, and her initials pressed faintly into the margin, not inked but dented into the paper as if the machine has learned the weight of her hand. [CLUE C004] Shaken by Marguerite’s fragments and the carbon copy, Iris recognizes the only ethical test available: she will not warn anyone about the slip, will not preemptively escalate without symptoms, and will not try to force the chart toward or away from the printed hour. She gives ordinary triage, routine monitoring, documented standard care, and nothing more. The patient survives past the printed time. Instead of relief, Iris feels a colder uncertainty, because the failed prediction does not prove the machine is harmless; it proves at least one slip can be wrong under certain conditions she does not yet understand. [ROMANCE] Because the canon has no real male lead, the required emotional micro-beat stays non-romantic: in the dangerous quiet before the printed time, Iris imagines the impossible steadiness of Unassigned beside her, then feels the tension and vulnerability of having no hand or shoulder to anchor her while she chooses restraint alone. Afterward, she returns to Marguerite and discovers an old logbook showing Marguerite once recorded a similar night of restraint in 1963, then abruptly stopped writing and soon quit nursing. The chapter ends not with an answer, but with a frightening parallel: Marguerite’s final legible note says only, 'The night I did nothing, the paper lied.'

chapter_plans.title: Iris Callahan at 05:19
chapter_plans.one_line_summary: With her own name printed, Iris realizes the machine’s final trap is to make her kill herself by fighting the label.
chapter_plans.beat_summary: Iris stares at the slip bearing her own name and 05:19, then begins the worst clinical assessment of her life: not of a patient, but of every decision she might make because she is afraid. R004 lands as a direct consequence of R003 and is set up through the prior evidence Iris already proved: C004 showed that a printed death can fail when she refuses to reshape care around fear, and C005 showed that hiding behind protocol can still become a lethal choice. The machine has turned its mechanism on Iris, and the danger is not a predetermined death but the cascade she will create if she panics, overcorrects, flees, doses herself, calls the wrong code, or forces the ER to move around her fear. The label has no room number, no patient category, and no triage mark, making Iris understand that the machine is naming the decision-maker as the next patient only if she lets terror turn her own body and shift into the site of harm. Marguerite, lucid in flashes, refuses to tell Iris what to do and instead admits she quit nursing because she could not bear responsibility after learning the same truth: the machine does not need to murder anyone when a frightened nurse will rearrange the night for it. Iris must keep working while watching the clock approach 05:19, choosing ordinary, measured action over desperate attempts to outmaneuver the slip. [ROMANCE] With no actual male lead, the required micro-beat is the painful absence of Unassigned at the moment of greatest fear: Iris almost turns as if someone could steady her shoulder, but there is only the counter, the paper, and the tension of needing comfort she will not invent. The chapter ends when a real emergency arrives minutes before the printed time, forcing Iris to choose between saving the patient in front of her and protecting herself from the label.

chapter_plans.title: The Choice That Remains
chapter_plans.one_line_summary: Iris treats the final emergency without obeying the machine’s trap, survives 05:19, accepts the preventable death in her past, and burns the printer until it falls silent.
chapter_plans.beat_summary: The final chapter continues from 05:16 as a cyanotic patient is rushed into the ER and the printer feeds its last label. Iris sees the trap clearly: if she lets her own printed time dictate the room, she will turn the emergency into the mechanism that kills her or someone else. She gives measured, ordinary care, refuses to flee, refuses to overcorrect, and accepts when the patient’s condition cannot be reversed despite correct treatment. [ROMANCE] With no true male lead in the canon, the emotional micro-beat remains the absence of Unassigned: at the height of fear, Iris briefly wants a steadying hand at her back, finds only empty air, and chooses to stand on her own without inventing romance. At 05:19, Iris is still alive. The printer does not triumph; it only sits there with paper in its teeth. Iris finally names the year-old death as preventable without letting the admission destroy her, then carries the machine to the hospital incinerator and burns it. The book closes with the machine silent, Iris no longer checking her pulse, and one charred slip surviving in the ash with her name and no readable date.
